name: Crystal arthritis (gout / pseudogout)

matching.reasoningTemplate: Acute mono/oligoarticular hot joint may be crystal-induced — but exclude septic arthritis by aspiration.

redFlags: Septic arthritis must be excluded by aspiration

clinicalPearls: Initial gout flares are usually monoarticular; the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases, followed by tarsal joints, ankles, and knees. Oligo- and polyarticular flares emerge over time (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Gout flares often begin at night to early morning, are among the most painful conditions humans experience, and the affected joint becomes warm, red, tender, and very swollen, frequently mimicking cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.2958).
Untreated flares usually subside spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, with symptom-free intervals (intercritical gout) until the next episode (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Serum urate can be normal or low during an acute flare because inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 are uricosuric and can lower urate by about 2 mg/dL; seek historical or post-flare urate values instead (Harrison 22e p.2959).

In CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) the knee is most commonly affected, followed by the wrist; the first MTP joint (podagra) is rarely involved, a useful distinguishing clue from gout (Harrison 22e p.2960).
Initial acute CPPD attacks tend to last longer than typical gout flares, sometimes weeks to months (Harrison 22e p.2960).
Acute CPPD can be precipitated by trauma, severe medical illness, or surgery (especially parathyroidectomy, which rapidly lowers serum calcium and magnesium and sheds crystals) (Harrison 22e p.2960).

Women account for only about 5-20% of gout patients; most are postmenopausal, elderly, and often on diuretics with coexisting osteoarthritis, hypertension, or mild renal insufficiency. Premenopausal gout is rare (Harrison 22e p.2958).
Hyperuricemia in a prepubertal boy should prompt consideration of inherited enzyme defects such as HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan spectrum) or PRPP synthetase superactivity (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) arthropathy can cause an extremely destructive arthropathy of the elderly, classically the shoulder (Milwaukee shoulder), with low synovial fluid leukocyte counts despite dramatic symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2961).

Hyperuricemia and gout are part of the insulin-resistance syndrome and associate with cardiometabolic-kidney comorbidities: obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, CKD, and urate nephrolithiasis (Harrison 22e p.2956).
harrison.pathophysiology: Gout arises from an increased body urate pool due to chronic hyperuricemia, leading to supersaturation and crystallization of monosodium urate (MSU) within joints and connective tissue. Hyperuricemia is predominantly due to impaired renal urate excretion (~90%) and less often urate overproduction (~10%); a minority (~10%) of cases reflect inherited metabolic disorders (PRPP synthetase superactivity, HPRT deficiency). Crystal shedding from inert synovial deposits, triggered by metabolic factors, diuresis, rapid urate changes (including urate-lowering therapy initiation), local trauma, or medical illness, activates resident synovial phagocytes (monocytes/macrophages, mast cells) and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta and other proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha). Phagocytosis of MSU crystals by neutrophils with a respiratory burst amplifies the acute inflammatory response. Persistent MSU deposition produces tophi (granulomatous inflammation around crystals) and chronic erosive gouty arthritis. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals; their release similarly drives inflammasome-mediated inflammation, analogous to hyperuricemia in gout. Apatite and calcium oxalate crystals can likewise stimulate synovial cell proliferation and release of proteases, collagenases, and prostaglandin E2, contributing to joint destruction (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962).
additionalDifferentials: Osteoarthritis - CPPD pseudo-osteoarthritis variant mimics progressive OA, often in atypical joints (MCP, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle) (Harrison 22e p.2960-2961)
Rheumatoid arthritis - chronic symmetric CPP synovitis can clinically resemble RA (Harrison 22e p.2961)
Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy - severe destructive CPPD may radiographically mimic it (Harrison 22e p.2961)
infectionMimics: Cellulitis - acute gout flare with warm, red, swollen periarticular tissue may mimic cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.2958)

Septic arthritis - crystal arthritis closely mimics it; aspiration with Gram stain and culture is essential, especially as bacterial infection can coexist with crystals in synovial fluid (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) mimics acute gout flares (Harrison 22e p.2960)
Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) deposition disease (Harrison 22e p.2961)
Calcium oxalate arthropathy - acute presentation may be indistinguishable from MSU, CPP, or apatite crystal disease (Harrison 22e p.2962)
additionalInvestigations: Polarized light microscopy of synovial fluid - MSU: needle/rod-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent; CPP: rhomboid/rod-shaped, weakly positively or non-birefringent; apatite: non-birefringent (requires alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy); calcium oxalate: bipyramidal, variable/strong birefringence, alizarin red S positive (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961-2962)
Synovial fluid Gram stain and culture to exclude coexisting septic arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961)

Synovial fluid leukocyte count - gout flare typically 5000-75,000/uL; acute CPPD ~24,000/uL (range several thousand to 100,000); apatite and calcium oxalate usually <2000/uL (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961-2962)
Arthrocentesis of an unaffected first MTP joint or knee between flares can still demonstrate MSU crystals (Harrison 22e p.2959)

Plain radiographs - advanced gout: well-defined erosions with sclerotic/overhanging margins, soft tissue tophi; CPPD: punctate/linear chondrocalcinosis in fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961)
Musculoskeletal ultrasound - double-contour sign over articular cartilage indicating MSU deposition; can also reveal chondrocalcinosis in CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961)
Dual-energy CT - identifies MSU crystals by chemical composition (Harrison 22e p.2959)
Baseline labs to assess comorbidities and treatment safety: serum creatinine, liver function tests, hemoglobin, WBC count, HbA1c, lipids (Harrison 22e p.2959)
In CPPD patients under 50, evaluate for metabolic/familial causes: serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, iron, transferrin (Harrison 22e p.2960)

HLA-B*5801 screening before allopurinol in high-prevalence populations (Southeast Asian, Pacific Islander/Native Hawaiian, Black patients) to reduce risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (knowledge point) (Harrison 22e p.2960)
redFlags: Crystal-proven arthritis does not exclude concurrent septic arthritis - bacterial infection can coexist with MSU or CPP crystals in synovial fluid; always Gram stain and culture (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961)

Acute CPPD can produce systemic features (fever, chills, raised acute-phase reactants), with low-grade fever in up to 50% and temperatures occasionally as high as 40C - mandates microbial culture to exclude infection (Harrison 22e p.2960, p.2961)
CPPD onset before age 50 warrants workup for underlying metabolic disease (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) or hereditary CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2960)
harrison.prognosis: Untreated gout flares typically resolve spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, but recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, joint deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Controlling the underlying chronic hyperuricemia (urate-lowering therapy to a subsaturation target) can prevent recurrent flares and dissolve tophi, generally requiring lifelong therapy. For chronic CPPD there is no means to remove established CPP crystal deposits from cartilage and synovium (unlike urate lowering in gout), and progressive destructive large-joint disease may require joint replacement. Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) progresses indolently and may also lead to joint replacement (Harrison 22e p.2958-2962).
pitfalls: Relying on a normal serum urate during an acute flare to exclude gout - urate is often normal or low at flare onset (Harrison 22e p.2959).
Attributing a destructive 'osteoarthritis' in atypical joints (MCP, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle) to primary OA rather than recognizing pseudo-osteoarthritis from CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2961).
Assuming chondrocalcinosis on imaging is always CPPD - calcium oxalate deposition in chronic renal failure is an exception (Harrison 22e p.2961).
Missing apatite arthropathy because individual apatite crystals are not visible on routine polarized light microscopy and need alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy (Harrison 22e p.2961).
Overlooking inherited enzyme defects when hyperuricemia/gout presents in a young patient, particularly a prepubertal boy (Harrison 22e p.2958).
